title: A Soft Fold
text:
Something gives way beneath you, the way a pillowcase gives when you finally find its opening. There is no fall. Only a long, slow *fwump*, like being folded by very patient hands, and then you are lying on grass the color of a baby blanket. Behind you, the fold still hangs open, breathing warm, dizzy air. You are alone. Folds deliver travelers one at a time, like a hand unloading a dryer.

The sky is lavender. Clouds tumble past, all one way, humming the low hum of a dryer on Delicate. A clothes peg signpost reads WELCOME, ODD ONES, and beneath it: *Everyone ends up here eventually.*

You check yourself for damage, then check your memories, which is scarier. *Pim. Right foot. Lilac. Calm as a folded towel. Survived a dog. Came home with me in a three-pack, one paper band round the middle.* All there.

You say it again, to be sure. It is a little quieter the second time.

choices.label: Follow the pastel path
Knock at the little cozy cottage
Wriggle back through, wherever it leads

title: The Pastel Plains
text:
The path is soft as a bath mat and winds through fields of dandelion fluff. Everywhere you look, socks are living their lives. None of them are with other socks.

A crew sock jogs past arm in arm with a shoelace. A knee-high naps in a hammock strung between two clothes pegs, curled around a sleeping oven mitt. Nobody seems to mind. Everybody seems, honestly, delighted.

A sundial in the middle of the meadow has no numbers, only little drawings of a dryer drum, each one turned a bit further. A sign beneath it says: *It is currently Cycle 4,112. Lunch is at Cycle 4,113.*

Three roads lead on. One smells of warm bread. One jingles. One climbs toward a tall, tall shape on the horizon that seems to be watching you.

choices.label: Follow the smell of bread
Follow the jingling
Head toward the tall shape

title: The Cottage of Mr. and Mrs. Argyle
text:
The cottage turns out to be a tea cozy, quilted and enormous, with a round door cut in its side. The door opens before you knock.

"A visitor!" cries an argyle sock in a tiny apron. Behind her, the cottage itself rumbles warmly. "Darling, we have a visitor!" "So I feel," says the tea cozy, from everywhere at once. You realize, with a little lurch, that the argyle sock is *married to the house*.

"We met three hundred cycles ago," Mrs. Argyle says, beaming, ushering you onto a cushion. "I was so lonely when I arrived. Now look at me. Never cold a day since." She pours something steaming into a thimble. "You look like you've come a long way, Stripes. Sit. Have some tea. Forget your troubles."

On the mantel, in a bottle cap frame, is a picture of an argyle sock exactly like her. "Who's that?" you ask. She peers at it fondly. "Do you know, I've never been sure."

choices.label: Sit down for tea
Thank them and head back out

title: Tea at the Cozy
text:
The tea tastes of fabric softener and summer afternoons. It goes straight to your toe. Mrs. Argyle tells you about the time she lost a button that wasn't hers, and the tea cozy chuckles so warmly the walls fog up.

"And who are you looking for, dear?" she asks. "My pair," you say. "My pair is called..." You stop. The name is right there, like a sock under the bed you can see but can't reach. It starts with a soft sound. P? B? Something calm.

"Oh, they all say that at first," Mrs. Argyle says kindly, topping up your thimble. "It passes. Everything here passes. That's the lovely thing."

The steam curls up between you, smelling exactly like being forgiven for something you can't remember doing.

choices.label: Have just one more cup
Ask the way home, quickly

title: Knit and Knead
text:
The bakery is run by a gym sock and a leather glove, and they are clearly, unbearably in love. The glove kneads dough with all five fingers while the sock rolls the loaves into shape by flopping on them. The sign above the door reads KNIT & KNEAD: BREAD FOR THE UNPAIRED.

"Fresh lint loaf?" the glove offers, holding out something golden and fuzzy. "Made from the finest dryer fluff. We get it delivered from the Trap."

The sock leans over the counter. "First time in the Dimension? You've got the look. Little bit frayed around the cuff." It squeezes the glove's thumb. "Don't worry. Everybody finds somebody here. Even if it's not who they were looking for."

Flour drifts down like the end of a tumble cycle. It is very cozy and it smells like staying.

choices.label: Ask if they've seen a lonely mitten
Offer to help with the baking
Ask who's in charge around here

title: The Other Mitten
text:
"A mitten?" The glove's fingers go still. "Red, with a snowflake on the back?"

It calls toward the back room, and out comes a small red mitten in a hairnet, dusted in flour. A snowflake on her back. A string trailing from her cuff, ending in nothing, exactly like Mitt's.

"Mitt?" she whispers. "I'm Mott. Last winter I blew off the sledding hill, rolled through half the town, and fell into a soft fold in a laundromat dryer. I thought Mitt had forgotten me. Everyone forgets, here." She presses a strand of red yarn into your cuff, unraveled from her own thumb. "Red yarn always finds the Return Spool. If you see Mitt, in here or out there, tell it the bakery's past the sundial. Tell it I'm *sorry about the snowball*."

You don't know what happened with the snowball. You decide that's between mittens.

choices.label: Follow the red yarn to the Spool
Ask her who rules this place

title: Second Batch
text:
You flop on dough. You are, it turns out, excellent at flopping on dough. The glove applauds with its whole self. The gym sock teaches you to brush the tops with melted fabric softener so they shine.

One batch becomes two. Two becomes six. Outside, the sundial ticks over by a whole cycle, then another, and you barely notice. It is warm in here. You are useful. Nobody is asking you where your pair is.

You catch your reflection in a baking tray and pause. Teal and mustard. Red heel. A little darn on the toe. For a second you can't remember why the darn makes you sad, or who used to tell you it didn't matter.

"Another batch?" the glove asks, beaming.

choices.label: Sure, one more batch
Step outside and follow the jingling

title: The Market of Spare Parts
text:
The jingling turns out to be a market, stalls made from upturned thimbles and matchboxes. Everything for sale is a single something. One earring. One cufflink. One contact lens, very proud of itself. "Loose buttons! Half a zipper! Get your strays!" shouts a vendor that is a single chopstick.

Above it all looms a clock tower, its face a round porthole of glass behind which a tiny drum turns and turns. "Don't stare at the Spin Clock," a passing mitten warns. "It tells you how long you've been here."

At the end of the row, a pincushion with a needle for a nose sits under a sign: DARNS REMOVED. GOOD AS NEW. Her customers come away smooth-toed and smiling and a little vague, like someone who has lost their keys and decided not to mind.

Your darned toe curls. Pim always said the darn didn't matter. That it meant somebody had loved you enough to mend you.

choices.label: Look up at the Spin Clock
Let the pincushion mend your toe
Let Vernon work the crowd

title: Market Intelligence
text:
"Leave this to me," says Vernon, rolling out of your cuff. "Markets are my people." He works the stalls like a politician, spinning on his edge, trading gossip for gossip, and comes back glowing.

"Okay. So. The big lady on the horizon, Madame Purl? Asks every newcomer three questions about their pair. Get them right, she sends you home. Get them wrong..." He jingles darkly. "Also, there's a pair out by the lighthouse in your exact stripes."

Then he stops. "Stripes. Quick. What year am I?"

"1998," you say. "Delaware."

"I *knew* that," he says, too fast. "I knew that." He has gone pale, for a quarter. "I've never had to ask before. This place wears the edges off you. Whatever we're doing, let's do it before I forget I'm money."

choices.label: Go and face Madame Purl
Head out to the lighthouse

title: Good as New
text:
The pincushion is very quick. A snip, a tug, a few clever stitches, and your toe is smooth and whole, as if nothing had ever worn through it. As if nothing had ever happened to you at all.

You feel wonderful. Light. New. You thank her and wander back into the market, admiring your perfect toe, and somewhere between the button stall and the chopstick you notice you have no idea where you were going. Or who you were going to.

Someone puts you on a stall. That seems right. A little card is pinned to your cuff: LEFT SOCK, STRIPED, LIKE NEW. Shoppers pick you up and put you down.

Sometimes, under the Spin Clock, you feel an itch on your toe where something used to be. You can never remember what. It was probably nothing. It was probably nothing at all.

title: The Spin Clock
text:
Behind the glass, a little drum turns. Beneath it, a counter rolls over with a soft click every rotation. Every sock who arrives gets a tally mark on the tower wall, and yours is already there, freshly chalked: *Stripes. Cycle 4,112.*

An old tube sock leaning on a cane joins you. "I count my cycles," it says. "Every one. That's the trick. The ones who stop counting forget where they came from. Then they forget what they came for." It taps its cane on the cobbles. "I came for a hiking boot. Can't remember its face. But I remember counting, and that's something."

It squints at your stripes. "Funny. There's a pair out at the lighthouse wearing your pattern exactly. Teal and mustard. Been here ages."

Your fibers stand on end. You start counting.

choices.label: Head out to the lighthouse
Go find whoever runs this place

title: Madame Purl
text:
Nobody rules the Odd Sock Dimension. But ask anyone anything, the way home, who's in charge, whether it's lunch yet, and they all point the same way: toward the tall shape on the horizon.

Up close, she is a sock puppet the size of a water tower, stitched from a thousand lost socks, argyle and athletic and fuzzy bedsocks, with dinner-plate buttons for eyes and a mouth that opens like the lid of a washer. Nobody's hand is inside her. Nobody needs to be.

"Ahhh," says Madame Purl, in a voice like every drawer closing at once. "A new one. Lovely stripes. Tragic darn. I am the Matchmaker, little left sock, and nobody here stays single for long. I have a *wonderful* partner in mind for you."

Behind her, a long queue of unlikely objects waits, each holding a tiny bouquet of lint.

choices.label: Hear the offers
Say you already have a pair

title: The Candidates
text:
Madame Purl presents them with a sweep of her heel.

First, an oven mitt, scorched in one spot, who promises you will never feel cold again and that he has been to Thanksgiving four times. Second, a single leather driving glove with a mysterious past, who says nothing at all but winks with its middle knuckle. Third, a tea cozy, round and quilted and patient, who simply says, "I'd keep you warm. I'd keep you so warm."

"The cozy," Madame Purl murmurs. "I've had my eye on the two of you for cycles. You'd be very happy, dear. Very, very happy. Happier than you've ever been in that cramped dark drawer."

The tea cozy rustles shyly. Somewhere far away, so faint you might be imagining it, you think you feel a calm right sock waiting.

choices.label: Say yes to the tea cozy
Decline. You already have a pair.

title: Prove It
text:
"Everyone has a pair when they arrive," Madame Purl says, not unkindly. "Then the cycles turn and the pair goes blurry, like a photo left in a pocket through the wash." Her button eyes catch the lavender light. "Three questions. Answer true and I'll show you the way home. Answer wrong, and well. Then you're already one of us."

The queue of suitors leans in. The tea cozy looks hopeful. Far off, a clock with a tiny drum for a face clicks over.

"First," says Madame Purl. "What is your pair *like*?"

You reach for the memory. It is thinner than it was when you landed, like a sock worn at the heel, and three answers rise at once, each one feeling a little bit true.

choices.label: Brave. Pim is scared of nothing.
Calm. Steady as a folded towel.
Anxious and fidgety, just like me

title: The Second Question
text:
Madame Purl's mouth twitches at the corner, which for a puppet her size is a seismic event. "Calm. Yes. I can see the shape of that in you. You lean on calm things."

The name comes back sharper: *Pim.* It lands like a dropped clothes peg, small and certain. Pim lying flat in the drawer while you fretted. Pim saying, "We always turn up."

"Second question," says Madame Purl. "Every sock who has been through something has a story. What did your pair survive?"

The tea cozy sighs and sits back down. The memory flickers as you grab for it: teeth or claws? Something with a wet nose, or something that purred?

choices.label: A cat. Pim survived a cat.
A lawnmower, somehow
A dog. Pim survived a dog.

title: The Last Question
text:
"A dog," Madame Purl repeats, and the whole queue of suitors gasps, because in the Odd Sock Dimension that is the stuff of legend. "Chewed, carried, buried under a cushion, and came out calm. Remarkable."

You glow a little on Pim's behalf. Pim never brags about it. You brag about it for both of you.

"Last one, little left sock, and it's the one nobody gets." The Matchmaker lowers her enormous head until her button eyes are level with your toe. "How many of you were there? When you were new, with the paper band still round your middles. How many came home from the shop together?"

Something old and quiet stirs in your weave. A thing nobody talks about.

choices.label: Three pairs. We came in a three-pack.
Two. Just Pim and me, always.
Six pairs, in a fancy gift box

title: Fading
text:
Something slips. It is the feeling of a stitch coming loose, very quietly, somewhere you can't see.

You try to think of your pair and get only a soft blur in a drawer, a vague warmth. Calm? Was it calm? There was a word for it. A short word, like a pin. Like a pin? The pastel light is so comfortable. The hum of the clouds is so steady. Whoever it was, they surely wouldn't want you to fret.

"There, there," someone says, and something soft and warm settles over you like a hug.

You look down at the darn on your toe. You have the oddest feeling it used to mean something.

choices.label: Let the name go
Cling to your darn and spin away
Count the cycles, like the old sock said

title: Counting
text:
You count. *Cycle 4,112.* It is like pulling a loose stitch tight. *4,113.* The blur gets an edge. *4,114.* A drawer. A lilac toe. A calm voice saying, "We always turn up."

You keep going, out loud now, the way the old tube sock taught you, and every number is a stitch the Dimension cannot quite pick out.

A shadow falls over you, tall as a water tower. Madame Purl has been watching the whole time.

"Counting," she says. "That old tube sock has been talking." Her button eyes narrow, not unkindly. "Very well. Once more, from the top. But only once, little left sock. Nobody gets three tries at their own heart."

choices.label: Face her questions again
Spin away while you still remember

title: Remembered
text:
"A three-pack," you say, louder than you meant. "One paper band. A striped pair, a lilac pair, and us: one of each, the pair that made no sense. The striped pair went missing our first winter. Nobody talks about it."

The silence is enormous. Then Madame Purl laughs, a sound like a whole load of towels falling out of a basket, and the suitors applaud politely and drift off home.

"Oh, you're a stubborn one," she says. "Good. Stubborn ones get home." She points one enormous heel at the horizon, where a great wooden spool turns slowly against the lavender. "The Return Spool. Every thread home is wound on it." Her other heel drifts, as if by accident, toward a lighthouse blinking at the far edge of the meadow.

Then she looks at you a moment longer than she needs to. Her stitches, up close, are very old and very tired.

choices.label: Take the Return Spool home
Follow her other heel to the lighthouse
Ask why she seems so tired

title: The Return Spool
text:
Every road home in the Dimension ends at the Return Spool. Up close it is a wooden spool taller than a laundry basket, humming like a dryer winding down, and its threads run out across the lavender sky into soft folds, each one quivering toward somewhere real.

One thread is warm and smells of fresh laundry: it tugs toward a basket of clean clothes. One is pulled tight and straight toward the foot of a tall wooden shape with drawers, and high at the top of it you sense, very faintly, something calm and patient. One is frayed and tangled and spins in lazy circles, and following it would mean starting over somewhere dark and warm and dizzy.

You grip the thread you choose with your whole cuff. The Dimension starts to fold itself up around you like a fitted sheet done properly, for once.

choices.label: Follow the warm thread to the basket
Follow the tight thread to the dresser
Grab the frayed thread and spin

title: The Lighthouse
text:
At the edge of the Dimension, where the pastel grass gives way to a sea of fluffy white, stands a lighthouse made from a rolled-up bath mat. Its light is a single bright lint ball, glowing.

Two socks are on the gallery, polishing the lamp. Teal and mustard stripes. Red heel patches. No darns at all. They look exactly like you, twice.

"Stripes?" says one. "*Little* Stripes? From the three-pack?" The striped pair: the one nobody talks about. They slipped through a fold together the first winter and never came back. "We built the lighthouse," the other says, "so anyone from our drawer who ended up here would see it and find us." They look you over. "You took your time. And you're alone. Where's Pim? Where's the lilac one?"

Your heart, which is mostly wool, does something complicated.

choices.label: Stay at the lighthouse with them
Ask them to come home with you
Ask them the way home

title: Keeping the Light
text:
"Come home with me," you say. "Both of you. The drawer has room."

The striped pair look at each other the way matched socks do, all at once. "The drawer," says one, slowly. "Was it the top one? Was it warm?" The other frowns. "There was a smell. Wood, maybe." They remember you perfectly. They remember Pim. They have kept the lamp lit so long that they have forgotten everything else, even the way back.

"Somebody has to keep the light on," the first says at last, gently. "For the next one of us who falls through." She pinches a spark of glowing lint from the lamp and tucks it into your cuff. "You go. Tell Pim we said the pair that made no sense was always the best one."

The spark is warm against your heel. The lamp turns its slow white circle.

choices.label: Carry the spark to the Return Spool
Stay and help keep the lamp lit

title: The Matchmaker's Secret
text:
Madame Purl lets out a long breath that ruffles the whole meadow. "Tired? Little left sock, I have been matching for ten thousand cycles. Every lonely sock who falls through, I find them someone. I make them happy." Her button eyes droop. "I never once found anyone for me. You can't match the matchmaker. Those are the rules."

She looks at you, at your stubborn stripes, your darn you've stopped hiding. "You remembered when nearly nobody does. That's what the job needs. Someone who knows what a pair is *for*." She holds out a knitting needle, long and silver and humming. "Stay. Take my needle. Let me finally rest. Or go home, and I'll keep stitching. Either way, I won't hold it against you."

The needle is warm. Pim is somewhere far away.

choices.label: Take the needle
Gently refuse and go home

title: Happily Cozied
text:
The wedding is held at Cycle 4,200 in the Pastel Plains. The gym sock and the glove do the cake: a three-tier lint sponge with fabric-softener icing. The Argyles are front row, crying. Your groom is a tea cozy, round and quilted and patient, the one Madame Purl always had her eye on for you. She officiates, booming over the meadow: "Do you, Stripes, take this tea cozy?"

You do. You honestly, gladly do. The cozy wraps around you and you are warmer than you have ever been, warmer than any drawer.

Sometimes, late in a cycle, you wake up with a word on the tip of your toe. Something short. Something calm. You lie there trying to remember who it belonged to, and then your tea cozy rustles in its sleep and pulls you closer, and the word drifts off like lint on a breeze, and you are happy. You are, strangely, completely happy.

title: Three of a Kind
text:
You stay. It isn't forgetting, not this time. You talk about Pim every evening on the lighthouse gallery, and the others tell you everything: how they slipped through, how they waited, how they kept the lamp lit for their drawer.

Every cycle, the three of you send a ribbon of light out across the fluffy sea, into every soft fold in reality, aimed at one particular dresser in one particular house. A beacon in teal and mustard. *We're here. We remember. Come when you're ready.*

It isn't the drawer. It isn't Pim. But it is family, the oldest kind, the kind that came home from the shop in the same paper band. And on clear cycles, when the beam reaches farthest, you swear you feel a calm little tug from very far away, as if someone on the other end is holding the light and not letting go.

title: The New Matchmaker
text:
You take the needle. Madame Purl sighs, and it sounds like a whole drawer settling, and then her stitches loosen one by one and a thousand old socks drift gently off across the meadow, free, each to its own wrong-but-happy home.

The needle teaches you everything. You learn to see the threads between things: the oven mitt and the dish towel, the lonely sock and the shy pot holder. You make them happy. You are very, very good at it.

Every new arrival, you ask the same thing first: "Tell me about your pair." And you listen, and you help them remember, and when they do, you send them home.

Sometimes, late in a cycle, you knit a single teal and mustard stripe and tuck it into the Return Spool, pointed at a dresser far away. You never forget Pim. That was the whole point.
